audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (antepenult default in 3+ syllables / initial in disyllables, with lexically marked exceptions; strict=false), with a caution note that Casad 1984 and Kim & Valdovinos 2014 treat stress as lexical with tone/laryngealization interactions — 'lexical' or 'conflict' if the catalog requires the modern description to govern.
audit.reasoning: Quote: verified verbatim in the now-held Preuss 1912 text at the cited pages. Source quality: the classification 'fixed-strict, dominant, antepenult' rests on a database pattern (StressTyp -> Gordon 2002) whose cited source (Casad 1984, held and read) gives no positional rule, backed up by a 1912 transcription-convention note that itself hedges ('sehr häufig', acute-marked exceptions, double-peaked words, fluctuating accent). Every later description of the same Jesús María variety points away from an exceptionless rule: Casad 1984 (phonemic tone partly independent of stress, primary+secondary stress, mobile-stress stems), and the instrumental pilot Kim & Valdovinos 2014 (fetched sources now), which assumes lexical stress, finds initial and final stress split roughly evenly across 117 monomorphemic disyllables from two speakers (22/50 and 37/67 final), and reports a stress-attracting prefix. sources.quote: "The dynamic accent is expressed by the acute ´. Very frequently it falls on the third-from-last syllable, for which reason in that case the marking of the accent is dispensed with. [...] If the accent falls on the first syllable of a disyllabic word, it is likewise not marked. [...] Some words are double-peaked, but no special mark for the second accent is used. The accentuation sometimes fluctuates in the same words."

sources.citation: Kim, Yuni & Margarita Valdovinos. 2014. The interaction of laryngealized vowels, stress, and falling pitch in Mariteco Cora. Proceedings of the Workshop on the Sound Systems of Mexico and Central America (SSMCA), Yale University, 12 pp. (fetched sources via Wayback copy of ling.yale.edu; live URL 404)
sources.quote: Instrumental pilot study of the same Jesús María (Mariteco) variety Preuss described. Treats Cora as having 'lexical stress' (following Casad n.d.); 'Disyllables introduce the dimension of stress to the analysis. Initial stress and final stress are both found. Cues include a high pitch prominence on the stressed syllable and devoicing of final unstressed vowels'. Counts for monomorphemic disyllables in isolation: younger speaker 28 initial-stressed vs 22 final-stressed (of 50); older speaker 30 initial vs 37 final (of 67). The definite prefix ɨ- attracts stress off the noun. No tonal contrast
sources.locator: abstract p.1; sec. 1.1 p.3 ('Because the definite article prefix [ɨ-] is stress-attracting, the noun loses its stress'); sec. 2.2 p.7 table (12)
